Tools & SystemsResearch framework · Coding pipeline · Bilingual web appLive · in course use

A teaching tool for game-design courses. Students analyse a difficulty mechanic from a game they know, and each analysis becomes coded, evidence-graded design guidance for small teams.

Problem
Difficulty advice for small teams is mostly opinion, and the sharp analyses students write for coursework get graded once and disappear.
Built for
Game-design instructors and their students first; indie developers as readers; in the long run, the game community itself as contributors and curators.
Approach
Each submission is split into statements, coded across three layers and seven negotiation dimensions, then clustered and weighed. A principle is published only when enough independent sources agree. Consent is kept separate from grading.
Where it's going
My thesis framework is the amniotic fluid, not the shell. Every claim it makes can be confirmed, revised or retired by the evidence, and the Vault is built to be handed to the community and outgrow it.
Result
Live and bilingual (EN / 中文): a mechanism library, an advisor that uses no AI, published guidance, and a public claims registry that shows its working.

Rendering & VisualsJavaScript · Canvas 2D · Unity URP · HLSLComplete · web and Unity

I wandered into Return of the Obra Dinn's 1-bit dither style by accident, then went back to reverse-engineer and verify it properly — now running live here and as a real-time shader in Unity.

Problem
Building this site's hero image, I wandered into an ink-on-paper dither look purely by feel — tuning cell size and contrast with no reference in mind, until I liked what came out. It wasn't until afterward that I placed it: the look matched Return of the Obra Dinn, a game I'd played years earlier. That recognition sent me back to study that specific game instead of just keeping my own made-up version.
Built for
Myself — a test of how far I could get reverse-engineering a well-documented rendering technique by eye before checking my work, and how far an AI-assisted workflow could carry graphics math I already know how to do by hand.
Approach
I reverse-engineered the look first, purely by comparison against memory — landing on an 8×8 ordered Bayer matrix on my own. Then I went to primary sources to check my work: Lucas Pope's own devlog confirms the 8×8 matrix and the threshold-compare method directly, and a technical write-up on reproducing the style fills in the piece I'd missed — a ~10% contrast boost applied before the threshold, pure black-and-white output, and no error diffusion (Floyd-Steinberg shimmers as the camera moves, ordered dithering doesn't). Sources below.
References
Lucas Pope, Obra Dinn devlog — TIGSource #32 (2017) — primary source for the 8×8 Bayer matrix and the threshold-compare algorithm.
kott, "The Obra Dinn Dither Style: Settings That Actually Reproduce It" — source for the ~10% contrast boost and the ordered-vs-error-diffusion reasoning.
Stuck on
My hand-reverse-engineered version looked fine sitting still but turned muddy wherever the lighting sat near the threshold — the contrast boost was the one piece I hadn't guessed, and research is what surfaced it. It's the whole difference between the two panels above.
Result
Both versions are done: the demo above runs live in the browser, and the same recipe runs as a real-time URP shader in Unity — an 8×8 Bayer matrix plus the contrast boost, ported from JavaScript into HLSL and wired up as a render-graph post-process feature.

2023 · Competitive & co-op board game · Print-and-play

A treasure-hunt board game for 2–4 players with two ways to win: a shared co-op victory or a solo one. Built with a five-person team; two rounds of playtesting with 36 players reshaped the action economy and turn pacing.

My partProject management and core mechanic design — I owned the rules, the board shape and the win condition, and ran and analyzed both rounds of user testing.
